Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 03:16-10:53. Connect
database, SQL and PostgreSQL vocabulary to the book's course.sales table. Follow SQL_Desk_Setup.pdf before
practising, not the old installer later in the video. Stop manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator,
runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
In M01 you opened a workbook and inspected records. A database also stores records, but you
ask a database engine to return the ones you need. You do not need to become fast at typing
before you can understand that idea. Today you will connect one SQL instruction to one visible
result and explain what is stored versus what is displayed. Complete G01 and the SQL Desk
Setup guide before running this lesson.
Imagine a shop with many years of records. Opening every record and finding each matching
sale by hand becomes awkward. A query expresses a question precisely enough that the
database can repeat the work. A data engineer will later put such queries inside dependable
processes. We begin with a question small enough to check with our own eyes.
Picture the arrangement
Object
Picture it as
In this course
Server
The program managing the
record store
PostgreSQL running on your laptop
Database
A separate collection of related
objects
standalone_de
Schema
A named area inside that
database
course
Table
Records with a defined set of
fields
sales
Query
A written request sent to the
engine
SELECT ... FROM ...;
Result
The rows returned for that
request
The grid below pgAdmin's editor
The filing-cabinet picture is only a mental aid. A schema is not a Windows folder you need to
create in File Explorer. In course.sales, the dot separates a schema name from a table name.
That spelling helps you choose the intended table even when other tables exist.
Our first training table deliberately has one item per order. Its grain is one row per order, and
order_id identifies that row. Real orders can have several items. M03 will give order headers and
item lines separate tables; do not assume this simplified M02 shape is a universal design.
Words before actions
A column is a named field such as quantity. A row contains the fields for one record. A data
type constrains which kind of value a column holds: text for IDs, integer for whole quantities,
numeric for prices, date for calendar dates, boolean for true/false, with NULL where a field may
be unknown. SQL means Structured Query Language. Execute means send an instruction for
the engine to carry out. The SQL editor stores the text you are preparing; the result grid shows a
previous execution until you run something again.
Follow with me once
In pgAdmin, open Query Tool on standalone_de. Type the following into a new editor tab. Select
all three lines and execute them as one statement.
SELECT order_id, item, quantity, unit_price
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id;
Read it aloud slowly: return the order ID, item, quantity and unit price from the sales table in the
course schema, arranged by order ID. SELECT introduces the requested output fields. Commas
separate those fields. FROM names the input table. ORDER BY requests a result order; we
deepen it in DE02-05. The semicolon marks the end of this statement. Line breaks make the text
readable but do not change its meaning here.
The first four results are the records you met in M01:
There are four additional records: 0011 Notebook, 0012 Pen, 0013 Ruler and 0014 Bag. The
whole result has eight rows and four columns. The table contains other fields, but the query did
not request them. Omitting customer_id from the display does not erase customer IDs from
storage.
What changed, and what did not
This SELECT reads data. It does not change a price or create a new sales table. If you close the
result tab and execute the same query again against unchanged inputs, the same requested
values return. Saving its text as a .sql file lets you repeat the request later; saving does not
freeze the source table. If a source changes later, rerunning the query can return a different
result.
Notice that order_id contains 0007, not the number seven used for arithmetic. Its type is text. A
price is numeric because multiplication and sums make sense for it. Even if a grid displays both
as characters on a screen, their database types and meanings differ. A result grid's formatting is
not the definition of a field's type.
If you are stuck
If there is no course.sales, use the setup guide's recovery table. If you see only one old result,
check which statement was selected and executed. If you wrote a comma after unit_price,
remove it: FROM is a clause, not a fifth selected column. If a column does not exist, compare its
exact spelling with the setup file. Do not rename a source column merely to make an accidental
spelling work.
Your independent practice
In a blank editor, request order_id and item from course.practice_sales, arranged by order_id.
Save the SQL and its output in DE02-01_attempt.sql and your study record. State the number of
rows and columns. Explain whether selecting only two fields deletes the others. You may consult
the new-words table, but first try to construct the request yourself.
Changed retry - after your first review
Use course.retry_sales. Request order_id, quantity and unit_price arranged by order_id. Explain
why the order ID and quantity have different roles even though both may contain digit
characters.
Ready-made revision
A query is a request; the result is its answer at execution time. course.sales names schema and
table. SELECT chooses displayed fields, FROM chooses input, and ORDER BY requests their
order. SQL text, stored table and displayed result are three different things. Teach it back: point
to each of those three objects in your own working session.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before
opening DE02-01 in the Explained Reviews book. After review, solve the changed retry and keep it as a
separate attempt.

Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 02:09:43-02:12:32. Watch
naming an output with an alias. Stop manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and
expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
You can now retrieve named fields. Next you will make the result easier for another person to
read and limit a preview to a few records. A preview is useful during inspection, but it is not a
total or a representative sample. Complete DE02-01 and keep the loaded tables unchanged.
Picture a printed delivery list with short labels. The label printed on the report need not be the
internal name on the warehouse shelf. An alias is that output label. LIMIT caps how many rows
the query returns. It does not mean the remaining records were deleted. These operations
change the result you request.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id AS sale_id, item AS product
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id
LIMIT 3;
The output headers are sale_id and product. Its rows are 0007 Notebook, 0008 Pen and 0009
Folder. AS introduces a temporary name for this output. The source column is still called item;
another query can still ask for item. A meaningful alias tells the reader what a field represents.
Use simple lowercase names with underscores so you do not need quoted identifiers at this
stage.
The database first has to determine which ordered rows belong at the front of this result. ORDER
BY order_id supplies that rule. LIMIT 3 then caps the output at three. Without ORDER BY,
PostgreSQL may return any three qualifying rows; the table has no promised physical row order
for your query to depend on. Running the same un-ordered query twice and seeing the same
rows does not turn an accident into a guarantee.
A useful preview versus a misleading conclusion
Suppose the first three products are Notebook, Pen and Folder. You cannot conclude that this
shop never sells bags. LIMIT did not inspect your question about all products; it deliberately
restricted the displayed records. The preview is useful for checking field names and typical
shapes. Later, COUNT and DISTINCT will answer specific whole-dataset questions.
For exploratory work, SELECT * requests all available columns. That can help you inspect a small
unfamiliar table. For the saved exercises and later transformations, name the fields you actually
need. If somebody later adds a column, a named field list makes your intended output clearer.
Avoid selecting a column just because it exists.
Small syntax details that prevent confusion
Single quotes create a text value. They do not ask for a column's contents. The next statement
returns the literal word item on every selected row:
SELECT 'item' AS literal_label, item AS actual_product
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id
LIMIT 2;
You should see item/Notebook and item/Pen. Read the first column as “the same label supplied
by this query.” Read the second as “the item stored in this record.” Some dialects accept
different alias quotation styles; the book consistently uses unquoted simple aliases and
single-quoted text values.
If you are stuck
No rows with LIMIT 0 is an intentional empty preview. Too few rows with LIMIT 100 can simply
mean fewer than 100 exist. An error after AS often means the alias contains spaces without
valid identifier quoting; change it to a simple name such as product_name. If you refer to
product in a later new query against course.sales, remember that product was an output alias,
not a source column you added.
Your independent practice
Return the first two course.practice_sales records ordered by order_id. Display order_id as
reference and item as product_name. Save the query and describe exactly what the limit
permits you to conclude about the number of records in the whole table.
Changed retry - after your first review
From course.retry_sales, return the last two IDs in descending order. Use the output label
reference and retain item. DESC after order_id asks for descending order. Explain whether a
second new query must use reference or order_id to select the original ID column.
Ready-made revision
AS names an output; LIMIT caps a result. Use ORDER BY whenever which limited rows appear
matters. SELECT item reads a column, while SELECT 'item' returns literal text. A preview is not a
row-count check, and an alias is not a permanent table edit.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before

Before starting: DE02-02. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform

Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 01:21:59-01:29:35. Watch
filtering and comparison operators. Read the book's quote rules and exact WHERE examples first. Stop manually
at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected. No
full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
A business question rarely asks for every record. “Which order lines cost at least 30 per unit?”
needs a rule for accepting or rejecting each row. You will express that rule with WHERE, inspect
boundary values, and distinguish a unit price from a line amount. Complete DE02-02.
Picture a checkpoint at which each record presents its unit_price. WHERE is the checkpoint rule.
A comparison tests two values. A predicate is an expression used as a true/false/unknown
test. SQL retains a row in WHERE only when the test is true. The unknown part becomes central
in DE02-06.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id, item, unit_price
FROM course.sales
WHERE unit_price >= 30
ORDER BY order_id;
Expect 0007 Notebook 49.50, 0010 Marker 30.00, 0011 Notebook 60.00 and 0014 Bag 250.00.
The marker passes because >= means “greater than or equal to.” With > 30 it would fail. Check
that boundary deliberately. A correct-looking list can still be wrong if a requirement said “at
least” and the implementation used “more than.”
WHERE appears after FROM and before ORDER BY. It does not require you to display the field
used in the filter, although displaying it during debugging is helpful. If the task asks about line
amount, unit_price alone is the wrong measure: two markers at 30 each have a line amount of
60. We will calculate that explicitly in DE02-07.
Text and date values
SELECT order_id, item, ordered_on
FROM course.sales
WHERE item = 'Pen'
ORDER BY order_id;
Expect 0008 and 0012. Single quotes tell SQL that Pen is a value. Without them, PostgreSQL
looks for an identifier named pen. Our examples use exact stored spelling, including capital P.
Do not assume every database uses the same rules for matching case. Text cleaning and case
handling come later.
A date condition uses a typed date literal:
SELECT order_id, ordered_on
FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on >= DATE '2026-09-03'
ORDER BY order_id;
IDs 0011 through 0014 match. DATE declares how to interpret the following year-month-day
text. That format avoids guessing whether 03/09 means March 9 or September 3. These stored
values are calendar dates without times; M03 treats timestamps separately.
Inspect a failure thoughtfully
Zero rows can be a valid answer. First check the exact literal and chosen source. If WHERE item
= 'pen' finds none, investigate case rather than deleting the predicate. If you see an old result
after a syntax error, the old grid is not the output of the failed query. Read Messages and rerun
after correction. Never judge a query by whether it returns some rows; judge whether those are
the intended rows.
Your independent practice
From course.practice_sales, show IDs, items and unit prices strictly greater than 30. Predict
which row at exactly 30 is excluded before you execute. Save the prediction and actual result.
Changed retry - after your first review
From course.retry_sales, return rows ordered before November 2, 2026, with ID and date.
Explain whether a November 2 record belongs in “before November 2.”
Ready-made revision
WHERE accepts individual input rows when its condition is true. Choose both the correct field
and the correct operator. Check an exact boundary value, use single quotes for text, and use
explicit year-month-day date literals. A successful execution can still answer the wrong business
question.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before
opening DE02-03 in the Explained Reviews book. After review, solve the changed retry and keep it as a
separate attempt.
Before starting: DE02-03. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: PostgreSQL Tutorial Full Course 2022, 55:48-58:12. Watch logical operators. The
book supplies explicit parentheses, truth reasoning and the NULL caveat. Stop manually at the listed end. Public
title, creator, runtime and published chapter boundaries inspected; full playback not verified.
Why this matters, and what you will do
“Paper or Writing products with quantities of at least two” contains two ideas. You will combine
them without accidentally letting some rows ignore the quantity rule. Complete DE02-03. This
skill matters because a wrong Boolean condition can silently admit the wrong records into a
later pipeline.
AND requires both tests to be true. OR accepts either true test. NOT reverses true and false; it
does not convert unknown into true. Parentheses mark which smaller question belongs
together. Picture two ticket checks: eligible category and sufficient quantity. Each row must
pass both overall checks.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id, category, quantity
FROM course.sales
WHERE (category = 'Paper' OR category = 'Writing')
AND quantity >= 2
ORDER BY order_id;
Expected IDs are 0007, 0008, 0010 and 0012. First ask whether each row belongs to either
selected category. Then ask whether its quantity reaches two. Folder 0009 and Notebook 0011
belong to Paper but have quantity one, so they fail the overall condition. Ruler 0013 has
quantity two but belongs to Tools, so it also fails.
Walk through the trap rather than memorising it
Without parentheses, AND binds more tightly than OR. That means the following query accepts
all Paper rows, or Writing rows that meet the quantity rule:
SELECT order_id, category, quantity
FROM course.sales
WHERE category = 'Paper'
OR category = 'Writing' AND quantity >= 2
ORDER BY order_id;
It returns six IDs: 0007, 0008, 0009, 0010, 0011 and 0012. The two quantity-one Paper rows
leaked through. Both queries execute; only the first matches our stated question. This is why
parentheses are not decoration. Write the grouped idea you intend, even when you could rely
on the language's precedence rule.
Now change the category check to NOT (category = 'Paper'). This means anything except Paper
for these non-null category values. It does not mean “find unknown category.” Missing-value
logic receives its own lesson next.
Your debugging routine
When a combined condition returns surprising rows, display each field used in the rule. Check
one accepted and one rejected row by hand. Then execute each smaller predicate separately if
needed. An elaborate condition is easier to understand when you can explain each part. Do not
keep swapping AND and OR until the count looks familiar; a count alone may hide a different
wrong set of records.
Your independent practice
In course.practice_sales, keep Paper or Bags rows with quantity exactly one. Show ID, category
and quantity. Write parentheses around the category condition and explain why P102 should not
remain.
Changed retry - after your first review
From course.retry_sales, return records that are not Paper and have quantity at least two. State
which two rules each returned row satisfies.
Ready-made revision
Translate the sentence into smaller tests before typing. AND requires both, OR permits either,
and NOT reverses a known truth value. Parentheses make the grouping explicit. Validate
membership with row IDs, not just an output count. Teach it back by explaining why 0009
leaked through the deliberately wrong guided query.
Evidence to keep: your attempt, the observed result and its explanation. Save the first attempt before
opening DE02-04 in the Explained Reviews book. After review, solve the changed retry and keep it as a

Before starting: DE02-04. Video: Instructor watch ranges appear below. Read the vocabulary, perform
the guided example and save an independent attempt before review.
Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 01:15:18-01:21:59. Watch
ORDER BY and DISTINCT. DISTINCT applies to selected tuples, not to a business claim that two records are the
same. Stop manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter
list inspected. No full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
A useful result must have a clear question, grain and ordering rule. You will sort with ties, list
unique combinations, and avoid hiding duplicate business records with DISTINCT. Complete
DE02-04. A repeated product name is not necessarily a duplicate sale.
Ascending means lower values first; descending means higher values first. A tie occurs when
sort values match. DISTINCT returns unique combinations of the selected output values. It does
not inspect your business definition of a duplicate. Picture the difference between a list of every
receipt and a catalogue listing each product once.
Follow with me once: deterministic inspection
SELECT order_id, item, quantity
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY quantity DESC, order_id;
0012 with quantity 4 comes first, then 0008 with 3. The quantity-2 rows are 0007, 0010 and
0013 in ID order, followed by 0009, 0011 and 0014 with quantity 1. The second sort key resolves
ties in the first. Without it, the database may put tied rows in any order. A second key is
especially useful before a LIMIT when the exact returned records matter.
ORDER BY changes result order, not the order of storage inside the table. A later query still
needs its own ORDER BY. DESC applies to the expression immediately before it; ORDER BY
quantity DESC, order_id means descending quantity and default ascending ID.
Follow with me once: the selected columns define uniqueness
SELECT DISTINCT item
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY item;
There are six products: Bag, Folder, Marker, Notebook, Pen and Ruler under the expected simple
alphabetical ordering. Your database's collation controls text sorting. Each product name
appears once, even though Notebook and Pen each occur on two sales records. The result grain
is now one row per distinct item name. No source sale was deleted.
SELECT DISTINCT item, unit_price
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY item, unit_price;
This returns eight combinations: Notebook appears at 49.50 and 60.00, while Pen appears at
10.00 and 12.50. Adding a selected column changes what DISTINCT compares. If you selected
order_id as well, every original sale would be distinct because its ID differs.
Why DISTINCT is not a universal repair button
Suppose a join later repeats the same order. Adding DISTINCT can hide repeated displayed
values while leaving the underlying modelling mistake unexplained. Worse, two legitimate sales
might display the same item and price and be collapsed unintentionally. First state what one
input and output row represents, identify the intended key, and investigate where repetition
arose. Use DISTINCT when the question genuinely asks for unique selected values.
Inspection you can perform now
Check that the chosen source is correct, list the output fields, inspect the first and last rows
under your intended sort, and count the small result by eye. For larger results we will use count
queries. If LIMIT is present, label the result a preview. A tidy grid is presentation; it is not proof
that filtering, grouping or uniqueness is correct.
Your independent practice
Return unique category names from course.practice_sales in ascending category order. Then
return its two highest unit prices with their IDs; break ties by ascending ID. Explain why the first
result has fewer rows than the source.
Changed retry - after your first review
Return distinct item and unit_price combinations from course.retry_sales. Then request the first
two records under descending quantity and ascending order_id. Explain how the second key
resolves the tied quantity of three.
Ready-made revision
ORDER BY belongs to a result request. Add a stable tie-breaker when exact ordering matters.
DISTINCT compares the whole selected combination, not just its first column. Unique products
and unique sales have different grains; fewer output rows can be correct for one question and
wrong for another.

Instructor demonstration: SQL for Data Analytics - Learn SQL in 4 Hours, 01:08:45-01:10:07. Short NULL
introduction; the book gives the full missing-value reasoning. Stop manually at the listed end. Public YouTube

Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 02:12:32-02:16:15. Watch
COALESCE. Substitute a value only when the meaning is justified, not to hide missing source data. Stop
manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected.
No full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
The shop knows that some orders were paid, knows that others were unpaid, and has not
recorded the answer for two orders. You will preserve those three states. Treating an unknown
payment as false would create a misleading unpaid list. Complete DE02-05.
A NULL marker represents missing or unknown information, not the text 'NULL', an empty
string, or the number zero. Comparisons involving a NULL generally yield unknown. WHERE
keeps only true results. IS NULL asks whether the marker is present. COALESCE chooses the
first non-null expression from its arguments; it is a fallback rule you choose, not a discovery of
the missing fact.
Follow with me once: find what is unknown
SELECT order_id, item, is_paid
FROM course.sales
WHERE is_paid IS NULL
ORDER BY order_id;
The returned IDs are 0010 Marker and 0013 Ruler. Their displayed Boolean cell may show [null]
or a blank depending on pgAdmin preferences. The SQL condition establishes its meaning.
Compare two questions:
SELECT order_id
FROM course.sales
WHERE is_paid = FALSE
ORDER BY order_id;
SELECT order_id
FROM course.sales
WHERE NOT is_paid
ORDER BY order_id;
Both return 0008 and 0012. Neither includes the two unknown records. NOT unknown remains
unknown; it does not become true. The complete partition is four paid, two unpaid and two
unknown records. We will express and total that partition with CASE later.
The common test that does not work
WHERE is_paid = NULL is not the missing-value test. The equality comparison is unknown for
each row, so WHERE keeps none. Even NULL = NULL does not establish equality between two
known values. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL for these questions. Do not put quotes around NULL
unless you truly mean the four-character text, which our Boolean column does not contain.
Follow with me once: a declared fallback
The discount field is missing for 0009. For this particular estimate, suppose the written business
rule says, “When the discount has not been supplied, display a provisional rate of zero.” Keep
the raw value alongside that estimate:
SELECT order_id, discount_pct,
COALESCE(discount_pct, 0) AS estimated_discount_pct
FROM course.sales
WHERE order_id = '0009';
The raw discount remains NULL; estimated_discount_pct is 0. This SELECT did not update
storage. The label estimated warns that zero came from an assumption. If the business has
supplied no fallback rule, keep the unknown and report the gap. Never silently convert a missing
payment status into unpaid merely because COALESCE can do it.
Recovery and validation
If you find zero missing records, inspect the exact predicate, source and current data. If your UI
hides null markers, deliberately run IS NULL rather than relying on appearance. If COALESCE
reports incompatible types, remember that all candidates must resolve to a suitable common
type: a numeric discount and the word Unknown cannot simply be mixed in a numeric
calculation.
Your independent practice
In course.practice_sales, separately return IDs with unknown payment and IDs with known
unpaid payment. Then display the raw and provisional-zero discount for its one missing-discount
row. Explain the assumption behind the provisional value.
Changed retry - after your first review
Use course.retry_sales. Return IDs whose customer_id is missing. Separately return IDs whose
discount_pct is missing. Explain why those need not be the same record.
Ready-made revision
Use IS NULL for missingness. Unknown, false, empty text and zero are different states. WHERE
retains true, not unknown. COALESCE applies an explicit fallback; preserve the raw value and
state any assumption. Teach it back: why does NOT is_paid exclude unknown payments?

Instructor demonstration: Learn PostgreSQL Tutorial - Full Course for Beginners, 02:16:15-02:20:21. Watch
NULLIF and division-by-zero protection. Our book distinguishes numeric division from integer division. Stop
manually at the listed end. Public YouTube title, creator, runtime and expanded publisher chapter list inspected.
No full-playback or transcript-completeness claim.
Why this matters, and what you will do
A unit price and a quantity become a line amount only after you specify the calculation. You will
calculate that amount, handle fractional division, and avoid converting an undefined ratio into a
believable number. Complete DE02-06. All course currency amounts are fictional INR; the
arithmetic does not include tax unless a task explicitly adds it.
An expression combines values and operators to produce a value. A cast requests a data type
conversion. A denominator is the divisor in a fraction. NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when a
equals b; otherwise it returns a. We use that last expression to mark a zero-denominator ratio as
undefined instead of dividing by zero.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id, quantity, unit_price,
quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id;
The eight gross amounts are 99, 30, 25, 60, 60, 50, 40 and 250. The first calculation is 2
multiplied by 49.50. Aliasing it gross_amount makes the unit and meaning clearer than an
automatically generated expression heading. Numeric output may include trailing zeros; 99.00
and 99 are numerically equal.
Multiplication takes place before addition unless parentheses say otherwise. A hypothetical
per-order fee of 20 added to a two-unit purchase at 49.50 is 2 * 49.50 + 20 = 119. The
expression 2 * (49.50 + 20) gives 139 because it applies the fee to each unit. SQL can execute
both perfectly. You must decide which matches the business rule. In M03 we will prevent real
order fees being repeated across multiple item lines.
A known discount and an unknown discount
For the provisional-zero rule stated in the previous lesson:
SELECT order_id,
quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount,
quantity * unit_price
* (1 - COALESCE(discount_pct, 0)) AS estimated_net
FROM course.sales
WHERE order_id IN ('0007', '0009')
ORDER BY order_id;
IN here means “equal to either listed ID”; DE02-13 deepens it. 0007 has gross 99 and estimated
net 89.10 with its known 10% discount. 0009 has gross and estimated net 25 under the
provisional-zero assumption. Omitting COALESCE would leave the second net NULL, honestly
reflecting the missing rate. Which version is appropriate depends on the declared purpose; the
estimated label matters.
Division: inspect the types
SELECT 1 / 2 AS integer_result,
1.0 / 2 AS fractional_result,
1.0 / NULLIF(0, 0) AS undefined_ratio;
PostgreSQL returns 0, 0.5 (possibly more decimal places), and NULL. Dividing two integers
truncates toward zero. Introducing a numeric operand keeps the fractional result. NULLIF turns
the zero divisor into a null marker, so the ratio is undefined instead of causing a division-by-zero
error. A later COALESCE to zero would assert a policy; it would not turn an undefined ratio into a
measured zero.
A weighted average later requires total value divided by total units, not the average of prices
regardless of quantity. At this stage, practise recognising the numerator, denominator and unit
before writing the expression. Use exact numeric types for these classroom currency amounts;
rounding a display is separate from choosing the underlying calculation.
If you are stuck
Wrong but plausible totals usually need inspection of the operands and parentheses. Show

Why this matters, and what you will do
The shop asks, “How many sales records do we have, and what is their total gross amount?” It
needs a summary rather than eight separate lines. You will choose an aggregate according to
the question and inspect how missing values affect it. Complete DE02-07.
An aggregate function combines values from several input rows into a summary. COUNT
counts, SUM adds, AVG computes an arithmetic mean, and MIN/MAX return the smallest/largest
non-null value. With no GROUP BY, the following request treats all qualifying inputs as one
group. Picture placing eight receipts into one envelope and writing a few summary facts on its
front. The envelope label is not another sale.
Follow with me once
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sale_rows,
COUNT(is_paid) AS known_payment_rows,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_total,
AVG(quantity * unit_price) AS mean_sale_amount,
MIN(unit_price) AS lowest_unit_price,
MAX(unit_price) AS highest_unit_price
FROM course.sales;
Expected: 8 sale_rows, 6 known_payment_rows, 614 gross_total, 76.75 mean_sale_amount, 10
lowest_unit_price and 250 highest_unit_price. The one output row represents the whole input
selection. It does not represent one of the eight original orders.
Check the total yourself: 99 + 30 + 25 + 60 + 60 + 50 + 40 + 250 = 614. The mean sale
amount is 614 / 8 = 76.75 because all eight line amounts are known. MIN(unit_price) answers a
per-unit price question, while AVG(quantity * unit_price) answers a per-sale amount question.
Similar-looking currency columns can describe different measures.
COUNT is two different questions
COUNT(*) counts input rows regardless of which fields are null. COUNT(is_paid) counts only rows
where is_paid has a non-null value. Both TRUE and FALSE count because both are known values.
It is not a count of paid orders. This distinction is easy to miss if a Boolean field looks like a
checkbox on the screen.
To count paid records alone, filter to them first:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paid_rows,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS paid_gross
FROM course.sales
WHERE is_paid = TRUE;
Expect 4 and 434. The records are 0007, 0009, 0011 and 0014. WHERE chooses records before
this aggregation. Two known-unpaid records total 80, and the two unknown-payment records
total 100. Their disjoint totals reconcile: 434 + 80 + 100 = 614.
Empty input is not the same as a measured zero
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_found,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_total
FROM course.sales
WHERE item = 'Laptop';
The result is one summary row containing 0 and NULL. COUNT reports no records; SUM has no
non-null values to add and returns NULL. If a report's agreed convention displays an empty
selection as zero, COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) can implement that convention. Keep COUNT alongside
it so “nothing observed” is not confused with records whose measured amounts add to zero.
Most ordinary aggregates ignore null input expressions. That does not mean they repair missing
source facts. If a rate is missing, calculating AVG over only known rates uses a different
denominator from assuming missing rates are zero. The business meaning determines which, if
either, is appropriate.

Why this matters, and what you will do
A grand total is useful, but the shop also wants total amount by product category. You will group
records, predict the new grain and reconcile category subtotals to the source total. Complete
DE02-08. GROUP BY is the SQL version of the grouping idea you used in a PivotTable, with an
explicitly written rule.
Picture sorting receipts into named trays: Bags, Paper, Tools and Writing. Each tray produces
one summary row. The number of trays is not the number of receipts. A grouping key defines
which tray a record belongs to. Grouped grain tells us what one resulting summary row
represents.
Follow with me once
SELECT category,
COUNT(*) AS sale_rows,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_total
FROM course.sales
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
Eight input sale rows become four category summaries. Check both kinds of reconciliation: 1 + 3
+ 1 + 3 = 8 records, and 250 + 184 + 40 + 140 = 614 currency units. Both checks matter. A
result can have the right grand total but mislabel a category, so also inspect at least one group
manually. Paper combines Notebook 99, Folder 25 and Notebook 60.
SELECT asks for the grouping key and aggregate values. GROUP BY category says that rows
sharing that category feed the same aggregate. ORDER BY category only arranges the resulting
summaries. Grouping and sorting are separate operations, even if a small result seems to arrive
sorted without an explicit request.
Adding a key changes the question
SELECT category, ordered_on,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_total
FROM course.sales
GROUP BY category, ordered_on
ORDER BY category, ordered_on;
The grain is now one row per category per date. There are eight such combinations in this
deliberately small dataset. Paper has separate summaries on September 1, 2 and 3. Adding
ordered_on did not merely provide a harmless descriptive label; it changed the grouping rule
and the output grain. In a larger source there might be many sales in each category/date
combination.
Conversely, trying to select an arbitrary item while grouping only by category makes
PostgreSQL ask you to resolve ambiguity. Which item should represent Paper: Notebook or
Folder? Our learning queries select grouping keys and aggregates explicitly. Do not add all
selected columns to GROUP BY automatically just to silence the error, because doing so can
change the intended question.
Where missing grouping values go
In PostgreSQL, rows with NULL for a grouping expression are collected into one null group. That
does not turn their unknown identities into one real known customer. A summary may
legitimately show “unknown customer” as a data-quality bucket, but you cannot infer that all
those records belong to the same person.

Why this matters, and what you will do
The shop now wants only categories whose combined gross sales exceed 150. That rule cannot
be applied to each sale independently: the combined category total does not exist until the rows
are grouped. You will choose WHERE for input-row rules and HAVING for group rules. Complete
Picture the receipt trays again. WHERE decides which receipts enter the room. GROUP BY puts
admitted receipts into trays. HAVING decides which completed tray summaries are shown. This
is a logical explanation of the query; PostgreSQL may choose a different physical execution plan
while preserving the requested meaning.
Follow with me once
SELECT category,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_total
FROM course.sales
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 150
ORDER BY category;
Bags 250 and Paper 184 remain. Writing 140 and Tools 40 are excluded. Paper qualifies even
though none of its individual sales exceeds 150. The distinction is the lesson: the condition
belongs to the group total.
Try expressing the wrong question deliberately:
SELECT category,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_total
FROM course.sales
WHERE quantity * unit_price > 150
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
Only Bags 250 remains because WHERE excluded every smaller sale before grouping. Paper
never had a chance to accumulate 184. This second query can be valid for a different question,
such as “category revenue from individually large purchases,” but it does not answer our first
one.
Use both clauses when the sentence requires both
Suppose the request becomes “Among paid sales, show categories with paid gross above 100.”
First filter individual records to known-paid, then group and filter summaries:
SELECT category,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS paid_gross
FROM course.sales
WHERE is_paid = TRUE
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) > 100
ORDER BY category;
Expect Bags 250 and Paper 184. Unknown-payment rows are excluded because the question
explicitly says paid. If the question concerned all sales, this filter would be inappropriate. A
correct query follows the actual question, not a habitual clause pattern.
The output alias paid_gross is useful in ORDER BY, but PostgreSQL does not generally let you
reference that SELECT alias in HAVING. Repeat the aggregate there, or later use a CTE to name
an intermediate result. If an instructor's MySQL query uses its aggregate alias in HAVING, use
the printed PostgreSQL form above.
Boundary and reconciliation checks
“Above 150” means > 150. “At least 150” means >= 150. Because HAVING intentionally
removes groups, the retained totals need not equal the original grand total. Check the full
grouped result before the HAVING filter, then check which groups the condition removes.
Reconciliation should respect the stage you are checking.

Why this matters, and what you will do
A payment flag is stored as true, false or unknown, but a report needs readable group names.
You will translate an explicit rule into CASE while preserving unknowns and checking that every
record goes into exactly one intended bucket. Complete DE02-10.
A CASE expression tests conditions in order and returns a value from the first matching
branch. WHEN states the condition; THEN states its result; ELSE supplies the fallback; END
finishes the expression. Picture a receptionist asking one question at a time and writing one
classification on a receipt. If the first question already accepts the receipt, later branches are
not used to reclassify it.
Follow with me once
SELECT order_id,
CASE
WHEN is_paid = TRUE THEN 'Paid'
WHEN is_paid = FALSE THEN 'Unpaid'
ELSE 'Unknown'
END AS payment_group,
quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id;
IDs 0007, 0009, 0011 and 0014 receive Paid; 0008 and 0012 receive Unpaid; 0010 and 0013
receive Unknown. Unknown does not satisfy either equality condition, so it reaches ELSE. Using
ELSE 'Unpaid' after only a paid test would merge missing evidence with known non-payment.
That is a data meaning error.
From row labels to a summary
The expression below counts true payment rows. Each qualifying row contributes the number 1;
every other row contributes 0:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN is_paid = TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
AS paid_rows,
SUM(CASE WHEN is_paid = FALSE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
AS unpaid_rows,
SUM(CASE WHEN is_paid IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
AS unknown_rows,
COUNT(*) AS all_rows
FROM course.sales;
Expected 4, 2, 2 and 8. Four plus two plus two equals eight. This is conditional aggregation:
each record contributes to an aggregate according to a condition. It makes the partition visible
in one row. For currency instead of counts, use quantity * unit_price as the contributing value in
each matching branch.
Ordered rules can overlap
Suppose “Large” means gross amount at least 100 and “Medium” means at least 50 but less
than 100. Test the larger threshold first:
SELECT order_id,
CASE
WHEN quantity * unit_price >= 100 THEN 'Large'
WHEN quantity * unit_price >= 50 THEN 'Medium'
ELSE 'Small'
END AS size_group
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id;
0014 is Large. 0007, 0010, 0011 and 0012 are Medium. 0008, 0009 and 0013 are Small. The
second condition can say >= 50 because amounts >= 100 have already matched the first
branch. Reversing the two WHEN clauses would label 250 Medium. A more verbose
non-overlapping rule can also be correct; clarity matters more than brevity.
CASE without ELSE returns NULL when no condition matches. That can be intentional, but here a
labelled Unknown or Small bucket is clearer. The branch outputs need compatible types; do not
mix a numeric amount with a free-text error message in a column that is meant to remain
numeric.

rule. Test overlapping thresholds in the intended order, include boundary cases, and reconcile
mutually exclusive categories. A friendly label is useful only if its rule is correct.

Why this matters, and what you will do
People type product labels differently, and dates need calendar-aware handling. You will
normalise simple text in an output without erasing the original, and extract parts of a genuine
date. Complete DE02-11. Deeper dirty-text and timestamp cases remain in M03.
A string is text. TRIM removes ordinary surrounding spaces by default; it does not remove
every possible invisible character or repair spelling. LOWER converts text to lowercase.
EXTRACT retrieves a date/time component. A date literal declares a calendar value; it is not
an arbitrary text format.
Follow with me once: keep source and cleaned value
SELECT source_id, item_raw,
LOWER(TRIM(item_raw)) AS item_clean
FROM course.raw_labels
ORDER BY source_id;
A contains two leading spaces and one trailing space around pen; it cleans to pen. B is PEN and
also becomes pen. C is empty text and remains empty. D is NULL and remains NULL. E becomes
note book, with the internal space preserved. F becomes pen blue, still with its two internal
spaces. This operation is deliberately limited: it makes surrounding whitespace and letter case
consistent, but it does not decide that Note book and Notebook mean the same product.
Keeping item_raw next to item_clean makes your change inspectable. You can explain why a
value changed rather than showing only the final label. The query has not updated the
raw_labels table. M03 adds a useful conversion of empty cleaned text into an explicit missing
marker.
Follow with me once: work with dates as dates
SELECT order_id, ordered_on,
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ordered_on) AS year_number,
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM ordered_on) AS month_number,
ordered_on + 7 AS follow_up_date
FROM course.sales
WHERE order_id = '0007';
Expect 0007, 2026-09-01, 2026, 9 and 2026-09-08. Adding integer 7 to a PostgreSQL date
means seven days. Calendar arithmetic handles month changes; editing the visible day digits
yourself would not. YEAR and MONTH are field names in EXTRACT, not quoted source column
names.
To select dates within September, use an inclusive beginning and an exclusive next-month
boundary:
SELECT order_id, ordered_on
FROM course.sales
WHERE ordered_on >= DATE '2026-09-01'
AND ordered_on < DATE '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY order_id;
All eight rows qualify. The pattern is called a half-open interval: the start is included and the
end is excluded. It also adapts well to timestamps, where “the last day” contains many times. In
this lesson ordered_on has no time component. Do not assume that every field displaying a
date-like value has the date type.

Alex's string lesson uses MySQL. LOWER, TRIM and common simple string ideas transfer, but
some function names and details do not. Use the PostgreSQL expression printed here. For
example, use EXTRACT(MONTH FROM ordered_on), not an assumed MONTH(ordered_on)
function. If a date cast fails, inspect the raw format before converting it; do not silently drop
inconvenient records.
If surrounding spaces seem to remain, first check whether you are looking at item_raw or

Some questions need the answer to another question first. “Which sales have amounts above
the average sale amount?” needs the average before it can decide which rows qualify. You will

checks. Complete DE02-12.
A subquery is a query nested inside another statement. A scalar subquery supplies one
value, such as an average. IN tests membership in a list or a one-column query result. EXISTS
asks whether a subquery returns any row; the actual selected value is not what it tests. Picture a
shop manager first writing the average on a note, then comparing each sale with that number.

FROM course.sales
WHERE quantity * unit_price > (
SELECT AVG(quantity * unit_price)
FROM course.sales
ORDER BY order_id;
The inner aggregate produces 76.75. The outer query returns 0007 with 99 and 0014 with 250.
Run the inner query separately first if the nesting feels unfamiliar. Its closing parenthesis marks
the end of the smaller request. Parentheses are not a new table and do not save that result
permanently.
Both references to course.sales are intentional: the comparison threshold and the candidate
rows use the same whole dataset. If you put a paid-only filter inside the subquery but not
outside it, you compare all candidates with a paid-only average. That may be valid, but it is a
different business rule. Always state the population used to calculate a threshold.
Membership and an existence question
SELECT order_id, category
FROM course.sales
WHERE category IN ('Paper', 'Tools')
ORDER BY order_id;
This returns 0007, 0009, 0011 and 0013. It is a shorter form of two equality conditions joined
with OR. An IN subquery must supply one comparable column for this simple scalar use; SELECT
* from a many-column table is not such a list.
SELECT EXISTS (
SELECT 1 FROM course.sales WHERE is_paid IS NULL
) AS has_unknown_payment;
The answer is true because at least one matching row exists. SELECT 1 is a conventional way to
say “any matching row is sufficient.” It does not count one row or return all matching IDs. M03
will use EXISTS to connect an outer record with matching inner records.
Why NOT IN needs missing-value care
Suppose a list contains C01 and NULL. For a different customer C02, the comparison with C01 is
false and the comparison with NULL is unknown. The database cannot prove that C02 is absent
from all list members, so NOT IN can yield unknown and remove a row you expected to keep.
For now, avoid building exclusion logic from nullable lists. In M03 we will use NOT EXISTS with an
explicit matching condition and separately discuss missing outer keys.

“More than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression” means the outer expression
needed one value but received several rows. Inspect the inner query by itself. Do not add LIMIT
1 simply to hide the problem: decide whether you needed an aggregate scalar, membership
with IN, or existence. A query returning a Boolean has a different purpose from one returning a
list of IDs.

Why this matters, and what you will do
Being able to repair and prove a small query is more useful than copying a longer one you
cannot explain. You will diagnose a plausible wrong result, separate syntax from meaning errors
and save reproducible evidence. Complete DE02-13. This is an integration lesson; use earlier
video segments as targeted refreshers after attempting the diagnosis.
A syntax error means the database cannot parse a statement as written. A semantic error
means the statement runs but answers the wrong question. Validation checks that the result
matches a stated contract: input, output grain, rules and important totals. A reconciliation
compares related counts or amounts expected to agree.
Start with a contract you can read aloud
The request is: “For known-paid sales only, return one row per category, show paid gross
amount, and keep categories with paid gross at least 100.” Before opening a query, identify the
input as course.sales, the row filter as is_paid = TRUE, the output grain as category, the
measure as quantity times unit price summed, and the threshold as a group rule. These five
choices give you something concrete to test.
A colleague offers this query:
SELECT category,
SUM(unit_price) AS paid_gross
FROM course.sales
WHERE is_paid IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(unit_price) >= 100
ORDER BY category;
It executes, but it includes known-unpaid records and sums prices without quantities. On our
source it returns Bags 250 and Paper 134.50. The presence of familiar category names does not
prove correctness. The word paid_gross is just an alias; SQL does not check that the formula
deserves the name.
Follow the repair one decision at a time
First inspect source IDs, quantities, prices and payment states. Correct the row rule to TRUE,
then calculate each row's amount, then group, then apply the group threshold. The repaired
query is:
SELECT category,
SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS paid_gross
FROM course.sales
WHERE is_paid = TRUE
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) >= 100
ORDER BY category;
Expect Bags 250 and Paper 184. A separate paid-source total is 434. Here both paid categories
pass the threshold, so displayed totals also sum to 434. That equality happens because no paid
category was filtered out; do not assume a thresholded result must always equal the full
paid-source total.

A useful small probe changes a boundary deliberately. In a new SELECT expression you can
compare 100 >= 100 with 100 > 100; there is no need to edit the source to test that operator.
For larger later pipelines, temporary tables and transactions will let us test changed inputs

Save evidence that lets you recover
Save the original query before repair, the exact database error or observed wrong result, the
corrected query, and one short explanation of each change. You can put SQL comments
beginning with -- above your query. You are documenting an actual attempt, not rewriting
theory notes. When asking for help, include the lesson ID, table name, query and exact error
text without a password. “It does not work” omits the information needed to diagnose it.
